newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ideas, anguish emerge in Algerian economic meeting.
newsitem.headline: Ideas, anguish emerge in Algerian economic meeting.

text.p: Algeria's seaside complex, Palais des Nations, will echoe on Thursday with ideas to restore the nation's battered industry, in debate marked by frankness on past mismanagement and fears and hope for the future.
On Friday, President Liamine Zeroual who summoned 500 people to give their ideas over five days, is expected, with Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia, to sum up. It will not be easy.
Algeria's oil and gas industry is outside the debate. It earns around $10 billion a year -- more than 95 percent of all foreign earnings.
"It seems imperative that Algerian industry manages, by itself, to release the resources for its own development," business confederation leader Said Nait Abdellaziz said.
Delegates - exministers, economic experts, representatives of groups like that for "victims of terrorism" and the powerful central trades union the UGTA - have all given prescriptions.

At stake are some 400 public companies employing around 1.7 million people. The problem is they produce at an estimated 35 percent capacity but have had about 500 billion dinars ($9 billion) pumped into them over the past seven years.
In the first half of 1996 industrial production fell seven percent compared with the same period last year.
Nait Abdellaziz said that within these groups were some 33,300 specialist, medium and small, firms employing 1.2 million workers, or 30 percent of the workforce.
Treasury director general Mohamed Younsi said public firms had not repaid either the treasury, or the banks, and in 1992, 1995 and 1996 there were major operations to help the companies
"Moreover, the treasury had bought back company bank debts. Besides the 670 billion dinars this cost, the treasury also disbursed 550 billion dinars," he said.
Delegates offered privatisation as one hope for the future -- but fears of job losses brought a warning from the UGTA trades union that it would always defend jobs.

The voice of the old-guard National Liberation Front (FLN), which ruled for over nearly three decades of socialism until 1991, also echoed through the hall. "The total and rapid abandonment of this sector would be a suicidal solution," its spokesman was quoted as saying by the official news agency APS.
Mohamed Liassine, a former industry minister up to 1997, said public firms should not be blamed for not "accumulating riches...the state banned this for more than two decades."
Algeria last week announced a privatisation council and delegates called for more encouragement for foreign investors.

The state oil and gas giant Sonatrach has signed more than 30 contracts with foreign firms willing to invest several billion of dollars in the North African OPEC member. But there has been little sign of interest outside the energy field.

The non-energy sector, with exports like small harvesters to places like Iraq, and dates, wine and scrap material, earned just $366 million in the first quarter of 1996. And this was a 53.4 percent rise over the same period the year before.

Ali Bekkouche, member of the National Economic and Social Council, said any strategy must "reduce the vulnerability of industry, increase output from installed capacity, reduce the technology delay and improve managemerial skills."
Other delegates saw Algeria's rescheduling of some $12 billion of its estimated $32 billion foreign debt as giving a breather to reorganise industry and management training.
A speaker for the legal Moslem fundamentalist party Hamas blamed lack of a national strategy for managing the debt.
"The economic problem will remain, for earnings will go inexorably in serving the debt," he said.
Algeria teetered near bankruptcy in 1994 when energy earnings were $8.4 billion and repayments without rescheduling would have totalled $9 billion.
Rescheduling brought debt serving down to 42 percent of earnings in 1995 and to 33 percent last year. But one senior Western diplomat said last week they would now start to rise.
On an optimistic note, management expert Aktouf Omar said: "To be non-industrialised is an advantage, we can profit from industrial countries' experience and not make the same errors."
